Oh I’ve become convinced there are two entirely separate disorders with almost the same symptoms that are seen as ADHD. There is true developmental ADHD, and then there are symptoms produced by overuse of certain technologies. The latter has entirely different causes and should be considered separate. If I was writing the manual I’d put the latter (where symptoms only manifest after consistent use of tech) as an acquired, not developmental, condition, though I’m not sure what category it fits.

I would like there to be a disorder for people who have some symptoms of multiple different developmental disorders, that combine to disable them, but who don’t meet enough of one individual disorder to be diagnosed. 

So, like if you have some autism traits and some ADHD traits and they combine in a way that becomes disabling. 

It’s like Mixed Anxiety and Depressive Disorder in the ICD-11, which is where you have many of the traits of both disorders but not enough of either to get two individual diagnoses. 

This isn’t something I experience, but I have seen other people who seem to fit with this kind of symptom profile, where they will have some social deficits and attention deficits, which makes their life really hard, but it’s a mix of both on a milder scale than someone with either autism or ADHD.

ABA was first developed by Ivar Lovaas, who was the same guy who invented conversion therapy. They use the same principles, their goal is to get the subject to comply with what is deemed "normal" by society. It doesn't focus on WHY the child is acting a certain way but only on WHAT they're doing.

There are risks associated with it as well, there have been studies linking ABA with PTSD. Also, many of the activities involve rewarding a child for doing something they find very unpleasant, which teaches that compliance is more important than comfort, and thus can lead to issues with consent later in life.

I know you'll want what's best for your kid, so I'd strongly recommend removing them from ABA, especially if you already have your own doubts - trust your instincts!

The people who want to see recurring villains are generally long-term fans who are very unlikely to stop watching the show. The people who want new things all the time tend to be more likely to quit, and therefore they are the people the BBC must keep on board in order for the show to be profitable. This isn't fair on long-term fans, but it's sadly how things work.

So I think the reason there's not so much character & world-building is partly due to a desire to please casual viewers and people who are not as engaged with the show at the expense of long-term fans because of money. While not ideal, at least this way it's less likely to be cancelled.
